subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Dark Matter: The Invisible Majority
description: A quick, practical guide to Dark Matter: The Invisible Majority.

hook.text: About 27% of the universe is dark matter. It doesn't emit or absorb light, and no one knows what it's made of.

buildup.text: Its gravity holds galaxies together and shapes the cosmic web. Without it, galaxies would fly apart.

discovery.text: Vera Rubin proved dark matter in the 1970s. Galaxy rotation curves showed stars moving too fast for visible matter alone.

twist.text: Decades of experiments have failed to detect dark matter directly. WIMPs, axions, and sterile neutrinos are all suspects.

climax.text: Dark matter makes up most of the matter in the universe—yet it remains the biggest unsolved puzzle in physics.

punchline.text: It shapes every galaxy. We feel its gravity. But we've never caught a single particle.

quiz.question: How did Vera Rubin provide evidence for dark matter?
options: Galaxy rotation curves showed stars moving too fast to be held by visible matter alone
She detected dark matter particles in a deep underground laboratory
She observed dark matter absorbing light from distant quasars

details.summary: Dark matter makes up roughly 27% of the universe's mass-energy content, yet it emits no light and interacts only through gravity. Its existence is inferred from galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing, and cosmic structure formation.
details.whyItMatters: Dark matter shapes the large-scale structure of the universe and holds galaxies together. Without it, galaxies would fly apart and the cosmic web would not exist as we observe it.
takeaways: Makes up about 27% of the universe's mass-energy
Detected only through gravitational effects on visible matter
Its true nature remains one of physics' biggest mysteries

faq.question: What are the leading dark matter candidates?
faq.answer: WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) have been the favored candidate for decades, though direct detection experiments haven't found them yet. Axions — extremely light hypothetical particles — are gaining attention.

faq.question: Could modified gravity explain dark matter observations?
faq.answer: Modified gravity theories (like MOND) can explain galaxy rotation curves without dark matter, but struggle with larger structures like galaxy clusters and the cosmic microwave background.
